location: Pacific Ocean, approximately 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California
the_unresolved_thing: Whether the mechanical stop (lower end play) fractured in-flight or upon impact, and the precise sequence of failure of the gimbal nut threads relative to torque tube fracture.

structural_test.why: The investigation did settle the primary mechanical cause (acme nut thread failure from insufficient lubrication), but early in the investigation a real disagreement existed over whether the mechanical stop broke in-flight (shifting liability toward Boeing design) versus on impact. The NTSB's final report attributes the uncontrollable dive to torque tube fracture followed by fairing bracket failure, but contemporaneous statements from Boeing and NTSB investigators reflect unresolved questions about exact sequence and timing.

commonly_wrong.claim: The mechanical stop (end play) broke off and that's what caused the uncontrollable dive.
commonly_wrong.record: The cause of the final dive was the low-cycle fatigue fracture of the torque tube, followed by failure of the vertical stabilizer tip fairing brackets, which allowed the horizontal stabilizer leading edge to move upward well beyond what a normally operating jackscrew assembly permits, creating excessive upward aerodynamic tail load and uncontrollable downward pitching.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: Collapses two distinct failure events into one, obscuring that the jackscrew's acme nut thread loss and the later structural fracture were separate stages of the accident sequence.

commonly_wrong.claim: The jackscrew itself broke during flight.
commonly_wrong.record: The acme nut threads on the jackscrew failed and stripped away. Later analysis estimated 90% of the threads in the acme nut had been previously worn away, and were completely sheared off during the accident flight.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The jackscrew (the shaft) survived; it was the acme nut riding on it that lost its threads. Confusing the two misattributes the failure mode.

commonly_wrong.claim: This was purely a random mechanical failure with no warning.
commonly_wrong.record: Two years earlier, a lead mechanic at Alaska Airlines' Oakland maintenance facility found the jackscrew end play worn to its maximum limit of 0.040 inch and ordered it replaced. The aircraft was returned to service days later with the worn assembly still installed.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: There was a documented maintenance flag on this exact assembly years before the crash, which matters for any claim that the failure was unforeseeable.

investigators_disagree.question: Did the mechanical stop (lower end play) fracture in-flight or on impact with the ocean?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB investigator Dan Bowers determined that re-creating the final part of the dive required tilting the stabilizer up 22 degrees, achievable only if the jackscrew separated from the end stop before impact.
investigators_disagree.position_b: Boeing spokeswoman Liz Verdier stated: 'Everyone agrees that it did break off but we don't know where' or when — leaving open whether it failed in flight or on impact.
investigators_disagree.status: The NTSB's final report settled on torque tube fracture and fairing bracket failure as the mechanism for the final uncontrollable dive, but the precise timing of end-stop separation relative to other failures was not conclusively fixed in contemporaneous investigative statements.

could_not_verify.item: Whether Alaska Airlines specifically used an unapproved type of grease on the jackscrew assembly (one source claims MIL-G-23827 instead of MIL-G-81322)
could_not_verify.note: Not directly quoted from NTSB AAR-02/01; only found in secondary sources.

could_not_verify.item: Exact details of the tools used in the end-play check and whether they were non-standard
could_not_verify.note: Mentioned in secondary sources but not directly accessed from the official docket.

could_not_verify.item: Specific words spoken by the pilots on the CVR transcript
could_not_verify.note: Only agency summaries of CVR content are available in these primary sources; any quoted dialogue would need direct docket transcript citation.

location: Bank of America branch, North Hollywood, Los Angeles
agency: Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD); incident response
the_number: 44 minutes duration; 2,000+ rounds exchanged; 11 officers and 7 bystanders wounded; 0 civilian/officer fatalities
the_unresolved_thing: LAPD patrol shotguns were restricted to buckshot-only ammunition at the time of the incident. No primary source—including the official LAPD Use of Force Review Board report filed June 12, 1998—documents who authorized this ammunition restriction, on what ballistic or policy grounds, or whether any safety recommendation about patrol armament standards was formally issued, accepted, or closed as unacceptable. The regulation permitting the condition that failed was never revisited or challenged in surviving official records.

structural_test.why: PASS—regulatory approval chain unresolved. The mechanism (buckshot cannot defeat rifle-rated body armor) is well understood; who set that ammunition policy and why is not.

commonly_wrong.claim: Officers were armed with rifles from the beginning of the encounter
commonly_wrong.record: Patrol officers initially carried only sidearms. Per the after-action report, officers did not confirm the suspects wore body armor until 9:33 a.m., roughly 16 minutes into the incident, then improvised by obtaining AR-15s from a nearby civilian gun dealer, B&B Gun Sales.
commonly_wrong.source: LAPD Use of Force Review Board Report, June 12, 1998
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The 16-minute gap is the entire structural failure the department later had to account for.

commonly_wrong.claim: The suspects used true armor-piercing ammunition
commonly_wrong.record: Media reported 'armor-piercing bullets,' but the robbers used standard high-velocity rifle ammunition—7.62×39mm and 5.56mm—not formally designated AP rounds. No independent ballistic test of the actual rounds used appears in the surviving docket.
commonly_wrong.source: Secondary reporting cross-checked against available docket materials; no ballistic test report located
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The gap between handgun and rifle rounds, not exotic ammunition, is what defeated patrol officers' weapons.

commonly_wrong.claim: SWAT rifles were immediately effective once they arrived
commonly_wrong.record: SWAT arrived 18 minutes after first shots. AR-15 fire had little effect on the heaviest armored areas; fatal hits came from unarmored zones—Phillips' hand and a self-inflicted head wound, Matasareanu's legs after a SWAT officer fired beneath a vehicle undercarriage.
commonly_wrong.source: Wikipedia summary cross-referenced with after-action narrative; primary ballistic detail not fully documented in surviving docket
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The ending is often flattened into 'SWAT rifles won'; the record shows armor gaps, not rifle superiority, ended it.

investigators_disagree.question: How many officers and bystanders were wounded?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NBC Los Angeles and Wikipedia: 11 officers, 7 bystanders wounded
investigators_disagree.status: Police1.com reports 11 officers, 6 bystanders; other outlets cite 12 and 8. The 1998 LAPD report should be the controlling figure, but public secondary sources have never converged.

could_not_verify.item: Exact ballistic specifications of the homemade body armor beyond 'Type III-A with trauma plate'
could_not_verify.note: No layer count, Kevlar weight, or construction detail located in primary sources.

could_not_verify.item: Whether the shotgun buckshot-only restriction was written policy or informal practice
could_not_verify.note: Central to the unresolved thread; stated as unresolved, not asserted either way.

could_not_verify.item: Any written LAPD safety recommendation on patrol rifle procurement or body armor threat assessment following the incident
could_not_verify.note: No such document located; absence itself is part of the unresolved claim.

could_not_verify.item: Federal data or inspection requirements attached to the 600 M-16 rifles the Pentagon supplied LAPD in fall 1997
Precise coordinates of where Matasareanu was cornered, roughly three blocks from the bank
could_not_verify.note: Not located in primary sources; bank coordinates used instead.

x_post: Everyone says LAPD officers were simply outgunned on Feb 28, 1997. The 1998 Use of Force Review Board report says something narrower: patrol shotguns were restricted to buckshot only. No surviving record says who set that restriction, or why it was never revisited.

hook_alternates.hook: Page one of the 1998 LAPD Use of Force Review Board report doesn't name who restricted patrol shotguns to buckshot.
Minute 16: officers confirm the robbers' armor stops their bullets. Minute 18: SWAT arrives with rifles.
LAPD had 600 military rifles within the year. On Feb 28, 1997, officers borrowed guns from a gun store.

longform_note: Long-form candidate: full docket exists (LAPD Use of Force Review Board Report, June 12, 1998), and the unresolved thread is institutional, not forensic—the ammunition-restriction approval chain, not the mechanics of the firefight. Structure the episode around the 44-minute timeline, then pivot at minute 30 to the open question: no surviving record shows who authorized buckshot-only patrol shotguns, whether any post-incident safety recommendation on patrol armament was issued, or whether it was ever closed. Avoid treating Phillips or Matasareanu's tactics as the causal center; the systemic gap is the armament policy, not the robbers' preparation.

location: Hudson River, Weehawken, New Jersey, opposite Intrepid Sea Air and Space Museum
the_unresolved_thing: The FAA approved the CFM56-5B4/P for service in 1996 under a bird ingestion standard that did not require testing for large birds on engines under 2.5 square meters inlet area, nor for core damage, nor for dual-engine failure scenarios. When Flight 1549 demonstrated that multiple large geese could destroy both engines simultaneously and cause total thrust loss at 2,800 feet, the NTSB recommended changes to that standard. For 13 years, no rule closed the gap between what the engine was certified to survive and what it met in service. The FAA's 2018 and 2023 rules changed the fan-speed condition for medium-bird testing. They did not extend large-bird testing to engines this size.

structural_test.why: The core mechanism, both engines losing thrust from a multiple large-bird strike, is settled and undisputed. What stayed open is regulatory: the FAA's 1996 certification of the CFM56-5B4/P exempted engines under 2.5 square meters inlet area from large-bird ingestion testing, and that threshold was never revised, even after the NTSB recommended it be reconsidered.

commonly_wrong.claim: Simulators proved Sullenberger could have made it back to LaGuardia; he chose the river instead.
commonly_wrong.record: Immediate-turn simulator runs succeeded in 7 of 13 attempts. The NTSB then inserted a 35-second delay to model real recognition and decision time. With that delay, 1 of 1 runs to runway 13 crashed short. US Airways testified a delayed return to runway 22 was never even attempted after the first four immediate-turn runs failed.
commonly_wrong.source: NTSB Docket SA-532, Exhibit 2DD Attachment 28, Simulator Results Document
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The clean version treats the ditching as a choice among equal options. The record shows the only tested return scenario with realistic delay ended in a crash.

commonly_wrong.claim: The bird strike was an act of God no regulation could have anticipated.
commonly_wrong.record: The CFM56 was certified in 1996 against medium and small flocking birds only, and was exempt from large-bird ingestion testing because its inlet area falls under the 2.5 square meter threshold. That exemption, not the bird strike, is what the NTSB targeted with recommendations A-10-64 and A-10-65.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: It reframes an engineering gap that was known and codified in 1996 as an unforeseeable event in 2009.

commonly_wrong.claim: All 155 survived because of the plane's design and luck.
commonly_wrong.record: The NTSB attributed survival to crew resource management, the captain's decision to ditch, and the aircraft's certification for extended overwater operations, including slide/rafts. The report noted that without that certification, 64 people on rafts would have faced 41-degree water, where cold shock and drowning can occur within five minutes.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: Luck did the work of the water and the ferries. The rafts and the ditching decision were a certification requirement and a testified judgment call.

investigators_disagree.question: Should engines with inlet areas under 2.5 square meters be required to pass large-bird ingestion testing?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB, May 2010: recommended the FAA re-evaluate the 2.5 square meter threshold entirely, finding the CFM56 core sustained severe damage from multiple large geese under a standard that never tested for it.
investigators_disagree.position_b: FAA, Federal Register, July 6, 2018: 'The evidence from the Flight 1549 accident did not indicate a deficiency in current bird ingestion requirements for the fan blades.' The FAA modified the medium-bird test speed instead of extending large-bird testing downward.
investigators_disagree.status: Recommendation A-10-64 closed with the 2023 fan-speed rule. The inlet-area threshold itself was never changed.

could_not_verify.item: Whether Airbus, before this accident, had flagged concerns about dual-engine bird strike vulnerability during high-altitude climb at reduced fan speed.
could_not_verify.note: No NTSB docket document or Airbus submission located that addresses pre-accident internal concern.

could_not_verify.item: Internal FAA or CFM documentation from the 1996 certification showing what dual-engine bird strike data, if any, was reviewed.
could_not_verify.note: No certification review file located in the public docket or Federal Register record.

slides.text: Every passenger and crew member aboard US Airways Flight 1549 survived the ditching in the Hudson River on January 15, 2009.
slides.visual: Full-bleed NTSB structures photo of the aircraft floating intact on the Hudson, cropped tight, no people visible.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: Simulators didn't clear LaGuardia
slides.text: Immediate-turn runs succeeded 7 of 13 times. With a realistic 35-second delay built in, the only completed run to runway 13 crashed short. A delayed return to runway 22 was never attempted after the first four tries failed.
slides.visual: NTSB Simulator Results Document, Exhibit 2DD Attachment 28, table of run outcomes with the delay column highlighted.

slides.label: What worked
slides.headline: The rafts were a requirement
slides.text: The A320 was certified for extended overwater operations, which meant slides that convert to rafts. The NTSB found that without that certification, 64 people would have faced 41-degree water where cold shock and drowning can occur within five minutes.
slides.visual: NTSB Structures Group photo of the intact fuselage and evacuation slides, Exhibit 7-A.

slides.label: The certification
slides.headline: "Did not indicate a deficiency"
slides.text: The CFM56-5B4/P was certified in 1996 against medium and small flocking birds. Engines under 2.5 square meters inlet area, like this one, were exempt from large-bird testing. In 2018 the FAA wrote that Flight 1549 did not show a deficiency in the fan blade requirements.
slides.visual: Federal Register notice, July 6, 2018, text excerpt rendered as a document scan with the quoted sentence boxed.

slides.label: The instant it read true
slides.headline: 80% fan speed, 2,800 feet
slides.text: The flight data recorder shows N1 and N2 on both engines degrading within seconds of the strike, at reduced climb fan speed, the exact condition the certification test never simulated.
slides.visual: NTSB FDR Factual Report chart, N1/N2 trace over time, Exhibit 10A.

slides.label: Why the standard held
slides.headline: The fan blades passed. The core didn't.
slides.text: FAA testimony at the June 2009 hearing traced the bird ingestion standard back through amendments in 2000 and 2007. Each revision addressed fan blade survivability. None addressed core damage from multiple large birds.
slides.visual: NTSB Public Hearing Transcript, Day 3, page excerpt on regulatory history, rendered as document text.

slides.headline:
1996: engine certified, large-bird exempt
2009: geese strike both engines at 2,800 ft
2010: NTSB recommends re-evaluating the exemption
2018: FAA declines, cites no fan blade deficiency
2023: new rule changes bird-test speed, not the exemption
slides.visual: Plain timeline graphic, no imagery, white text on black.

slides.text: 150 passengers, 3 flight attendants, 1 first officer, 1 captain. No fatalities were recorded in this accident.
slides.visual: Black slide, white serif numeral, no names listed, no photographs.

slides.label: Unresolved
slides.headline: The exemption is still on the books
slides.text: The 2.5 square meter inlet threshold that excused this engine from large-bird testing in 1996 has never been revised. The FAA's 2023 rule changed the fan-speed condition for medium-bird tests. It did not require large-bird testing on engines this size.
slides.visual: Split frame: 1996 certification standard text beside the 2023 Federal Register rule text, no imagery.

source_line: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-10/03, May 4, 2010; NTSB Docket SA-532, public hearing transcripts June 2009; Federal Register notices 2018 and 2023; FAA Lessons Learned database.

155.

Every person aboard US Airways Flight 1549 survived the ditching in the Hudson River on January 15, 2009. The engines that failed had been certified in 1996 under a standard that exempted engines their size from large-bird ingestion testing, a standard the FAA never fully revised.

NTSB/AAR-10/03; Docket SA-532; Federal Register 2018, 2023.

x_post: US Airways 1549's CFM56 engines were certified in 1996 against medium and small birds only. Engines under 2.5 sq meters inlet area, like this one, were exempt from large-bird testing. That exemption is still in the rulebook.

hook_alternates.hook: FAA, 2018: "The evidence... did not indicate a deficiency in current bird ingestion requirements."
14 years between the recommendation and a rule. The rule didn't touch the exemption.
The NTSB said re-test the threshold. The FAA changed the fan speed instead.

longform_note: Tier C. The failure mechanism (dual bird strike, both engines) is fully settled and not disputable. The long-form hook, if this case is ever revisited for A-tier treatment, is the 2.5 square meter certification threshold itself: why it was set there in 1996, what data supported it, and why 13 years of recommendation traffic never touched it. That paper trail (FAA rulemaking docket, CFM/Airbus certification basis documents) was not available in this research pass and would need to be pulled before any long-form claim is made.
